Photograph: Dawid Wolski/East News/Shutterstock Melbourne The gunzels’ grand final: Melbourne Tramaroos’ campaign derails at European TramDriver Championship The Warsaw event saw 26 teams compete across a series of demanding tasks, inspired - to varying degrees - by tram drivers’ day-to-day tasks Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Petra Stock Sun 20 Sep 2026 04.16 EDT Last modified on Sun 20 Sep 2026 04.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google It’s the grand final for gunzels. But despite having one of the largest tram networks in the world, Melbourne’s Tramaroos finished second last at this year’s European TramDriver Championship, just ahead of London. The event, held in Warsaw on Saturday, saw 26 teams compete across a series of demanding tasks, inspired – to varying degrees – by tram drivers’ day-to-day work. In smooth stop and go, drivers travelled with a bowl of water attached to the front of the tram – with points deducted for every drop spilled. Other precision tasks involved speed control at 25 km/h, target braking, tram bowling, lateral distance, basketball, a perfect stop with the second door, and a reverse ride guided by whistle commands. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Daniel Bowen, a spokesperson for the Public Transport Users Association, said it was “an unusual event in the pantheon of world sports”. “It’s pretty entertaining,” he said, and an opportunity to look for inspiration from great other tram systems around the world. “Everyone looked like they were having a great time.” View image in fullscreen The basketball component. Photograph: Dawid Wolski/East News/Shutterstock This year’s title went to Vendula Tmejová and Zdeněk Rychtář, from Prague, in the Czech Republic. In 2022, Australia was the first ever non-European country chosen to participate. This year, Yarra Trams sent Ivan Cavanagh of Southbank depot and Claudia Barrientos from Kew depot to compete as the “Tramaroos”. Had they won , the trophy would have gone “straight to the pool room”, Cavanagh said. “You would hope our team would do well but I’m sure there’s pretty stiff competition against you know the Europeans,” Bowen said. “Perhaps it’s a bit like Eurovision – it’s great to participate .” View image in fullscreen A member of the Danish team from Odense celebrates after their final run. Photograph: Wojtek Radwański/AFP/Getty Images Thousands of fans followed the spectacle live in Warsaw, with about 80,000 viewers worldwide watching the competition via livestream. Melbourne is set to host the next event in 2027. Bowen said it would be interesting to see if other Australian cities joined the competition, given recent extensions to light rail systems in Adelaide, Sydney, Canberra and the Gold Coast. “Back in Melbourne, it’s a reminder that trams do form a vital part of the transport system. We do have the biggest tram network in the world, but there’s more to do in terms of accessibility and on-road priority and service frequency.” Explore more on these topics Melbourne Transport news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Speaking to reporters, Tomczyk explained that pilots currently must not only rely on radar readings but also establish visual contact with an object before shooting it down; this entails flying up to the target to identify exactly what it is. Now, the Polish Ministry of Defense plans to scrap the visual identification requirement. Tomczyk noted that, once the changes are implemented, a pilot or commander will be able to decide whether to shoot down an object based solely on radar data. The new rules will save time, meaning Polish fighter jets will be able to shoot down drones and missiles coming from Russia more quickly. On the 23rd of September, a Russian Mi-8 helicopter briefly entered Polish airspace from the Königsberg region. It penetrated about 300 meters into Polish airspace and remained there for 42 seconds. Poland responded by scrambling fighter jets. The Polish Operational Command commented on the incident, noting that Russia was once again testing the readiness of Poland's air defenses. Poland has previously shot down drones that entered its airspace. Around this time last year, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski stated that Poland would shoot down Russian fighter jets if they crossed the airspace border, adding that the Russians had been warned.
